title: Vishnu Sahasranamam Lyrics with Meaning: Verses 91-92
desc: Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 91 to 92 in Sanskrit with a simple English meaning and how to chant them: 'भारभृत्कथितो योगी योगीशः सर्वकामदः'.
alt: Lord Vishnu, Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 91 to 92 with meaning
caption: Vishnu Sahasranamam, verses 91 to 92.
intro: **Vishnu Sahasranamam** is the thousand names of Lord Vishnu, taught by Bhishma to Yudhishthira in the Mahabharata. This post gives **verses 91 to 92** with the Sanskrit text and a plain English meaning, so you can chant with understanding.
takeaways: The verses here open with **भारभृत्कथितो योगी योगीशः सर्वकामदः**.
Read the Sanskrit slowly, then the meaning, then chant once more.
Thursday and Ekadashi are the days most families keep for Vishnu Sahasranamam.
A short daily portion is better than a rushed full reading.

p: Read the lines aloud, one breath for each half of a verse:
**भारभृत्कथितो योगी योगीशः सर्वकामदः । आश्रमः श्रमणः क्षामः सुपर्णो वायुवाहनः ॥** **धनुर्धरो धनुर्वेदो दण्डो दमयिता दमः । अपराजितः सर्वसहो नियन्ताऽनियमोऽयमः ॥**

He carries the burden, his glory is sung, the yogi and lord of yogis, who grants every wish. The shelter, the one who strives, the lean, the winged one, whose vehicle is the wind, is that God of gods. He bears the bow, he is the science of archery and the rod of justice. The one who tames and self-restraint itself is that God of gods. Undefeated, bearing all, the controller, beyond every rule and beyond even death.
Light a lamp, sit facing east and chant these verses once, then read the meaning silently. Many families take two verses a day and finish the full text in a little under two months.
The names do not need a long ritual. What matters is steady practice, a clear pronunciation and a calm mind.

ul: Thursdays, the day of Vishnu and the planet Jupiter.
Early morning after a bath, or in the evening at the lamp.

faq.q: What do Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 91 to 92 mean?
faq.a: He carries the burden, his glory is sung, the yogi and lord of yogis, who grants every wish. The shelter, the one who strives, the lean, the winged one, whose vehicle is the wind, is that God of gods. He bears the bow, he is the science of archery and the rod of justice. The one who tames and self-restraint itself is that God of gods. Undefeated, bearing all, the controller, beyond every rule and beyond even death.
**Bhishma** taught it to Yudhishthira on the field of Kurukshetra, as told in the Anushasana Parva of the Mahabharata.

faq.q: Can I chant a few verses a day instead of the whole text?
faq.a: Yes. A small daily portion with the meaning understood is a common and accepted way to learn it.

note: The Sanskrit is the traditional text. The English is our own plain rendering of the meaning.
